entries.lesson_core_move: State the convolution theorem as the operational equivalence between continuous-time convolution and Fourier-domain multiplication, connecting direct LTI output convolution to frequency-domain signal analysis.

sections.section_title: Recognizing the Time-Domain Convolution Side

prompt_blocks.text: Given $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p(\tau)q(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, which option is the matching compact time-domain convolution notation?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The integral already has the standard convolution pattern: one signal is written as $p(\tau)$, the other is shifted to $q(t-\tau)$, and the result is integrated over $\tau$.
So the compact time-domain convolution notation is $y(t)=p(t)*q(t)$. The other choices are pointwise multiplication, a correlation-like shift, a sum, or the Fourier-domain product.

prompt_blocks.text: Which integral is the expanded time-domain convolution form of $y(t)=m(t)*n(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The compact notation $y(t)=m(t)*n(t)$ expands to the standard convolution integral with one signal written as $m(\tau)$ and the other shifted to $n(t-\tau)$.
That is the time-domain convolution form. The other choices are pointwise multiplication, subtraction, a correlation-like shift, or the Fourier-domain product.

sections.section_title: Stating the Matching Fourier-Domain Product

prompt_blocks.text: If $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, what is $Y(j\omega)$ in the Fourier domain?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a time-domain convolution, so the convolution theorem says to switch to the matching frequency-domain product.
That product is the Fourier-domain expression for the output spectrum.

prompt_blocks.text: If $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, what is $Y(j\omega)$ in the Fourier domain?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The integral is just the convolution written out in full, so the same theorem applies.
So the matching Fourier-domain output is the same product of the two spectra.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Theorem as an LTI Output Relationship

prompt_blocks.text: For an LTI system with input $u(t)$ and impulse response $g(t)$, which statement correctly interprets the convolution theorem for the system output?

choice_blocks.text: The same output can be written as $y(t)=u(t)*g(t)$ in time and $Y(j\omega)=U(j\omega)G(j\omega)$ in frequency.
The same output can be written as $y(t)=u(t)g(t)$ in time and $Y(j\omega)=U(j\omega)+G(j\omega)$ in frequency.
Time-domain multiplication becomes frequency-domain convolution, so $Y(j\omega)=U(j\omega)*G(j\omega)$.
The theorem only gives the time-domain form $y(t)=u(t)*g(t)$ and does not describe the output spectrum.
The theorem makes $U(j\omega)$ and $G(j\omega)$ the outputs, while $Y(j\omega)$ is the input spectrum.

questions.correct_answer: The same output can be written as $y(t)=u(t)*g(t)$ in time and $Y(j\omega)=U(j\omega)G(j\omega)$ in frequency.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The theorem gives two equivalent descriptions of one LTI output: convolution in time and multiplication in frequency. The other choices either reverse the theorem, drop one of the two descriptions, or confuse the roles of input, impulse response, and output.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose $x(t)$ and $h(t)$ are the input and impulse response of an LTI system. Which statement best explains how the theorem helps with output analysis?

choice_blocks.text: It gives two equivalent descriptions of the same output, so you can use $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$ for direct computation or $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ for spectral analysis.
It says time-domain multiplication becomes frequency-domain convolution, so $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)*H(j\omega)$.
It only gives the time-domain output $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$ and does not say anything about frequency.
It only gives $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ and does not connect that to the output.
It swaps the roles of $x(t)$, $h(t)$, and $y(t)$, so the output spectrum becomes the input spectrum.

questions.correct_answer: It gives two equivalent descriptions of the same output, so you can use $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$ for direct computation or $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ for spectral analysis.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The theorem does not replace one view with the other; it says they describe the same LTI output. That is why the time-domain form is useful for direct computation and the frequency-domain form is useful when spectral analysis is clearer.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert y(t)=x(t)*h(t) into Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega) to represent a convolution-based LTI system output in the Fourier domain.

sections.section_title: Transforming y(t)=x(t)*h(t) into the Output Spectrum

prompt_blocks.text: If an LTI output is $r(t)=p(t)*q(t)$, which expression equals $R(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency, and the output keeps its label on the left.
The other choices either add, divide, multiply in time, or put the expression in the wrong domain or without the output label.

prompt_blocks.text: For the LTI output $z(t)=m(t)*n(t)$, what is its Fourier-domain form?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The convolution theorem converts the time-domain convolution into a product in the frequency domain, with the output label preserved.
The other options divide the spectra, drop the output label, use time-domain multiplication, or put the expression in the wrong domain.

sections.section_title: Transforming h(t)*x(t) into the Same Product Spectrum

prompt_blocks.text: If an LTI output is $y(t)=h(t)*x(t)$, which expression equals $Y(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because convolution is commutative, $h(t)*x(t)$ is the same LTI output as $x(t)*h(t)$. The Fourier transform of that output is still the product of the two spectra.

prompt_blocks.text: If the same output is written as $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, which expression equals $Y(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Swapping the convolution order does not change the output because convolution is commutative. The Fourier-domain output is still the product of the input and impulse-response spectra.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Convolution Integral into a Product Spectrum

prompt_blocks.text: If $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}a(\tau)b(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, which expression equals $Y(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The integral already matches the convolution form, so the output spectrum is the product of the two individual spectra.
The other choices either add the spectra, keep the time-domain integral, or drop one factor.

prompt_blocks.text: If $r(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p(\tau)q(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, which expression equals $R(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The integral is still a convolution, just with different signal labels, so the Fourier-domain output is still the product of the two spectra.
The wrong answers either add the spectra, use time-domain multiplication, keep the integral form, or omit one factor.

sections.section_title: Identifying X(j\omega)H(j\omega) as the Fourier Transform of x(t)*h(t)

prompt_blocks.text: Which time-domain signal has Fourier transform $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A product in the Fourier domain corresponds to convolution in time, so $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ comes from $x(t)*h(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which time-domain signal has Fourier transform $H(j\omega)X(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The order of multiplication in the Fourier domain does not change the result, so the time-domain signal is still a convolution: $h(t)*x(t)$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the pointwise product X(j\omega)H(j\omega) and interpret its magnitude and phase as the Fourier-domain representation of the time-domain convolution x(t)*h(t).

sections.section_title: Pointwise Multiplication of X(j\omega) and H(j\omega)

prompt_blocks.text: Given $X(j\omega)=4e^{j\pi/4}e^{-j\omega/3}$ and $H(j\omega)=5e^{-j\pi/6}e^{j\omega/3}$, what is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ after simplifying?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply the magnitudes to get $4\cdot 5=20$. Then add the phase exponents: $j\pi/4-j\pi/6=j\pi/12$, and the $\omega$ terms cancel because $-j\omega/3+j\omega/3=0$. So $Y(j\omega)=20e^{j\pi/12}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $X(j\omega)=2e^{-j\pi/5}e^{j\omega/4}$ and $H(j\omega)=3e^{j\pi/10}e^{-j\omega/6}$, what is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ after simplifying?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply the magnitudes to get $2\cdot 3=6$. Combine the phases: $-\pi/5+\pi/10=-\pi/10$, and combine the $\omega$ terms: $\omega/4-\omega/6=\omega/12$. So $Y(j\omega)=6e^{j(\omega/12-\pi/10)}$.

sections.section_title: Magnitude of a Frequency-Domain Product

prompt_blocks.text: If $X(j\omega)=4e^{-j\pi/4}e^{-j\omega}$ and $H(j\omega)=5e^{j\pi/8}e^{j2\omega}$, what is $|Y(j\omega)|$ for $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the magnitude rule: $|Y(j\omega)|=|X(j\omega)||H(j\omega)|$. The complex exponentials have unit magnitude, so only the coefficients matter.

prompt_blocks.text: If $X(j\omega)=(1+\omega^2)e^{j\pi/6}$ and $H(j\omega)=2e^{-j\pi/3}e^{-j\omega/2}$, what is $|Y(j\omega)|$ for $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same magnitude rule. The phase factors do not change magnitude, so multiply the magnitudes only.

sections.section_title: Phase of a Frequency-Domain Product

prompt_blocks.text: For $X(j\omega)=4e^{-j\pi/3}e^{j\omega/2}$ and $H(j\omega)=3e^{j\pi/6}e^{-j\omega/4}$, which expression gives the simplified phase of $Y(j\omega)$ for $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For a product, phases add pointwise in $\omega$. The coefficients $4$ and $3$ do not contribute phase, so read the two phase terms directly.
Add the phases and simplify.
So the simplified phase is $\omega/4-\pi/6$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $X(j\omega)=-2e^{j\pi/5}e^{-j\omega}$ and $H(j\omega)=5e^{-j\pi/2}e^{j\omega/3}$, which expression gives the simplified phase of $Y(j\omega)$ for $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The negative real factor in $X(j\omega)$ contributes a phase shift of $\pi$. Then the phases add pointwise in $\omega$.
Add those phase terms and simplify.
So the simplified phase is $7\pi/10-2\omega/3$.

sections.section_title: Reading X(j\omega)H(j\omega) as the Spectrum of x(t)*h(t)

prompt_blocks.text: If $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$, which statement correctly interprets $Y(j\omega)$ in this lesson?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The lesson reads the pointwise product in frequency as the spectrum of the convolution output. So $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ corresponds to $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, not to time-domain multiplication or a sum.

prompt_blocks.text: If $Y(j\omega)=6e^{j(\omega/2-\pi/6)}$, what does this expression represent in the context of the lesson?

choice_blocks.text: It is the Fourier-domain spectrum of $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$.
It is only one factor of the output spectrum, not the full product.

questions.correct_answer: It is the Fourier-domain spectrum of $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The simplified expression is still a frequency-domain product. In this lesson, that means it represents the spectrum of the convolution output $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, with the magnitude and phase read from the product.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compare y(t)=x(t)*h(t) with Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega) by deciding which domain gives the clearer computation or interpretation of an LTI system output.

sections.section_title: Matching y(t)=x(t)*h(t) with Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)

prompt_blocks.text: Which frequency-domain expression matches the output of the LTI system described by $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The time-domain output is $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, and its frequency-domain form is the product $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$. Convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency, so the output spectrum is the product of the input and impulse-response spectra.

prompt_blocks.text: For $r(t)=a(t)*b(t)$, which frequency-domain expression matches the output?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The letters change, but the rule does not. The time-domain convolution $r(t)=a(t)*b(t)$ becomes the frequency-domain product $R(j\omega)=A(j\omega)B(j\omega)$, so the output spectrum is still the product of the input spectrum and the impulse-response spectrum.

sections.section_title: Choosing Time-Domain Convolution for Overlap and Support Questions

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-3)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$, which domain gives the quickest route to the support of $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signals have finite support, so the support of $y(t)$ is easiest to read by sliding one pulse across the other and tracking overlap. That is a time-domain convolution question, not a frequency-domain algebra question.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=u(t-1)-u(t-4)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$, which domain gives the clearest route to the overlap interval of $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Overlap intervals are read directly by sliding the finite pulses across each other in time. The time domain makes that geometry visible immediately, while the frequency domain adds extra algebra that is not needed for the support question.

sections.section_title: Choosing Frequency-Domain Multiplication for Algebraic Computation

prompt_blocks.text: For $X(j\omega)=\frac{3}{1+j\omega}$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{5}{2-j\omega}$, which domain gives the quickest route to $Y(j\omega)$?

choice_blocks.text: Time-domain convolution, because the output must be found by integrating overlap in time.
Frequency-domain multiplication, because the spectra are already algebraic and the output is just their product.
Time-domain support analysis, because only the overlap interval matters here.
Interpreting the output spectrum qualitatively without computing it.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that both inputs are already given as algebraic spectra. That makes frequency-domain multiplication the clearest route, because $Y(j\omega)$ is found by direct product rather than by setting up a time-domain convolution integral.

prompt_blocks.text: For $X(j\omega)=\frac{2}{2+j\omega}$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{3}{2-j\omega}$, which expression is the simplified form of $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply the algebraic spectra directly. The frequency-domain route is the clearest one here because the output is just a product of two rational expressions.
Since $(2+j\omega)(2-j\omega)=4+\omega^2$, the simplified product is $\frac{6}{4+\omega^2}$.

sections.section_title: Choosing the Clearer Domain for Interpreting an LTI Output

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has input $X(j\omega)$ and a low-pass $H(j\omega)$ that strongly suppresses high-frequency components. Which domain gives the clearest interpretation of the output?

choice_blocks.text: Time domain, because the output is still a waveform.
Frequency domain, because $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ shows the low-frequency content passing and the high-frequency content being suppressed.
Both domains equally, so neither is clearer.
Time-domain overlap, because the filter effect is best seen by shifting signals in time.
Frequency domain, but only because multiplying spectra is easier than convolving signals.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is spectral filtering, not time-domain overlap. That makes the frequency domain the clearest choice, because $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ shows which spectral parts pass and which are suppressed.
Because $H(j\omega)$ is small at high $|\omega|$, the output keeps the low-frequency content and removes the high-frequency content. That is the interpretation the frequency domain makes immediate.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has a deep notch in $H(j\omega)$ around $\omega_0$, and the input spectrum has energy near that band. Which domain gives the clearest interpretation of the output?

choice_blocks.text: Frequency domain, because the notch in $H(j\omega)$ directly shows which band is removed from $X(j\omega)$ and how that shapes $Y(j\omega)$.
Time domain, because the output is still a waveform.
Both domains equally, so neither is clearer.
Time-domain overlap, because the support picture is the only thing that matters.
Frequency domain, but only because multiplying spectra is simpler than convolving signals.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a notch in $H(j\omega)$ around $\omega_0$. That makes the frequency domain the clearest choice, because the product shows directly which band is removed from $X(j\omega)$.

A deep notch means the output spectrum loses energy near $\omega_0$ while the rest of the spectrum remains. The time domain still describes the same output, but it is less direct for explaining the band removal.

entries.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
entries.lesson_core_move: Trace the proof idea of the convolution theorem by substituting the convolution integral into the Fourier transform definition, interchanging integration order, and recognizing the two individual spectra.

sections.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
sections.section_title: Substituting the Convolution Integral into the Fourier Transform

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression correctly rewrites the transform after substituting the convolution definition for $(x*h)(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The only move here is to replace $(x*h)(t)$ with its integral definition. Keep the outer Fourier kernel $e^{-j\omega t}$ outside, and do not change variables or the order of integration yet.

prompt_blocks.text: If $Z(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(f*g)(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$, which expression correctly substitutes the convolution definition for $(f*g)(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute the convolution integral for $(f*g)(t)$ and keep the outer transform integral unchanged. The kernel $e^{-j\omega t}$ stays outside, and the order of integration does not change yet.

sections.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
sections.section_title: Rewriting the Transform as an Iterated Integral

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression correctly rewrites the substituted Fourier transform as a double integral with separate $t$ and $\tau$ roles?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Flatten the nested structure into a double integral without changing the integrand. The outer Fourier kernel stays attached to $t$, and the inner integral still uses $\tau$.

prompt_blocks.text: If the same rewrite is written with dummy variables $u$ and $v$, which expression correctly puts it in double-integral form?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Renaming the dummy variables does not change the structure. The correct rewrite still keeps the kernel on the outer variable and flattens the nested integral into a double integral.

sections.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
sections.section_title: Interchanging the Order of Integration

prompt_blocks.text: Which rewritten form correctly interchanges the order of integration in $Z(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}u(\tau)q(t-\tau)e^{-j\omega t}\,d\tau\,dt$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Choice A is correct because $u(\tau)$ depends only on the outer variable, so it moves outside the inner $t$-integral while the rest of the integrand stays unchanged.

prompt_blocks.text: Which rewritten form correctly interchanges the order of integration in $W(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p(\alpha)r(t-\alpha)e^{-j\omega t}\,d\alpha\,dt$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Choice B is correct because the factor $p(\alpha)$ depends only on the outer variable, so it stays outside while the inner integral remains with respect to $t$.

sections.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
sections.section_title: Exposing the Shifted Transform Factor

prompt_blocks.text: Which rewrite correctly exposes the shifted transform factor after substituting $u=t-\tau$ in the inner integral?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Let $u=t-\tau$, so $t=u+\tau$ and $dt=du$. The exponential becomes $e^{-j\omega t}=e^{-j\omega(u+\tau)}=e^{-j\omega\tau}e^{-j\omega u}$, which exposes the shift factor.
The wrong choices either flip the sign, drop the exposed factor, or replace $H(j\omega)$ with the wrong transform term.

prompt_blocks.text: For $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}g(t+\tau)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$, which rewrite correctly exposes the shift factor after the substitution $u=t+\tau$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Let $u=t+\tau$, so $t=u-\tau$ and $dt=du$. Then $e^{-j\omega t}=e^{-j\omega(u-\tau)}=e^{+j\omega\tau}e^{-j\omega u}$, so the shift factor is positive in the exponent.
The distractors either flip the sign, drop the exposed factor, or change the transform factor to the wrong frequency form.

sections.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
sections.section_title: Recognizing the Product of the Two Individual Spectra

prompt_blocks.text: If $Y(j\omega)=\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)e^{-j\omega\tau}\,d\tau\right]H(j\omega)$, which final identification correctly states the convolution theorem?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The outer integral is exactly $X(j\omega)$, and the exposed factor is $H(j\omega)$. So the convolution theorem statement is the product $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $Z(j\omega)=G(j\omega)\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}u(\tau)e^{-j\omega\tau}\,d\tau\right]$, which identification correctly turns the factorized expression into the theorem statement?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The factorized outer integral is $U(j\omega)$, and the remaining factor is $G(j\omega)$. Multiplying the two named spectra gives the theorem statement $Z(j\omega)=U(j\omega)G(j\omega)$.

entries.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a continuous-time LTI convolution problem into Fourier-domain multiplication by finding X(j\omega) and H(j\omega), simplifying Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega), and inverse-transforming to recover y(t).

sections.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
sections.section_title: Translating a Convolution Output into Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)

prompt_blocks.text: A system output is written as $z(t)=p(t)*q(t)$. Which frequency-domain equation matches the convolution theorem?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The time-domain statement is a convolution, so the convolution theorem turns it into a product in the frequency domain. The output spectrum stays on the left, and the input and impulse-response spectra multiply on the right.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI output is written as $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$. Which equation is the correct frequency-domain statement for $Y(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The integral is the convolution form of the output, so the theorem says to replace it with multiplication in the Fourier domain. That gives the output spectrum $Y(j\omega)$ as the product of $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$.

sections.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
sections.section_title: Finding X(j\omega) and H(j\omega) from Transform Pairs

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t)=2e^{-t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, which pair of transforms is correct before forming $Y(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the standard pair $\mathcal{F}\{e^{-at}u(t)\}=\frac{1}{a+j\omega}$ and keep the factor 2 on $x(t)$. That gives $X(j\omega)=\frac{2}{1+j\omega}$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2+j\omega}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t)=e^{-2(t-1)}u(t-1)$ and $h(t)=3e^{-t}u(t)$, which pair of transforms is correct before forming $Y(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A delay by 1 multiplies the transform by $e^{-j\omega}$, so the shifted exponential becomes $X(j\omega)=\frac{e^{-j\omega}}{2+j\omega}$. The factor 3 stays with the impulse response, so $H(j\omega)=\frac{3}{1+j\omega}$.

sections.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
sections.section_title: Simplifying the Frequency-Domain Product Y(j\omega)

prompt_blocks.text: Given $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{3}{2+j\omega}$, which simplified form of $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ is ready for inverse transformation?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply first to get $Y(j\omega)=\frac{3}{(1+j\omega)(2+j\omega)}$. The goal is to rewrite that product in a standard inverse-transform form.
Choice B is correct because it keeps the factor 3 and splits the result into two familiar transform-pair terms. The other choices either leave the product unsimplified or change the algebra.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $X(j\omega)=\frac{2+j\omega}{1+j\omega}$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$, which simplified form of $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ is ready for inverse transformation?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use $(2+j\omega)=(1+j\omega)+1$ to separate the repeated factor.
Choice A is correct because it rewrites the product as a sum of standard terms ready for inverse transformation. The other choices either stay unsimplified, drop a term, or change the coefficient.

sections.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
sections.section_title: Inverse-Transforming Y(j\omega) to Recover y(t)

prompt_blocks.text: Given $Y(j\omega)=\dfrac{3}{1+j\omega}-\dfrac{2}{4+j\omega}$, which time-domain signal is $y(t)$ after inverse transformation?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match each term to the inverse pair $\mathcal{F}^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{1}{a+j\omega}\right\}=e^{-at}u(t)$ and keep the coefficients attached by linearity.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $Y(j\omega)=e^{-j3\omega}\left(\dfrac{1}{2+j\omega}+\dfrac{4}{5+j\omega}\right)$, which time-domain signal is $y(t)$ after inverse transformation?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The factor $e^{-j3\omega}$ delays the time signal by $3$, and each rational term matches $\mathcal{F}^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{1}{a+j\omega}\right\}=e^{-at}u(t)$.

sections.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
sections.section_title: Applying the Full Shortcut to an LTI System Output

prompt_blocks.text: For the LTI system with $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$, use the convolution theorem to choose the correct output $y(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The transforms are $X(j\omega)=1/(2+j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)=1/(3+j\omega)$. Multiplying gives $Y(j\omega)=1/((2+j\omega)(3+j\omega))=1/(2+j\omega)-1/(3+j\omega)$, so the inverse transform is $y(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)-e^{-3t}u(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: For the LTI system with $x(t)=2e^{-t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, use the convolution theorem to choose the correct output $y(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Here $X(j\omega)=2/(1+j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)=1/(2+j\omega)$. Their product is $Y(j\omega)=2/((1+j\omega)(2+j\omega))=2/(1+j\omega)-2/(2+j\omega)$, so the time-domain output is $y(t)=2e^{-t}u(t)-2e^{-2t}u(t)$.
